title: ECE 302: Introduction to Electrical Engineering
text: In Fall 2024, Chris studied introductory circuit analysis in ECE 302 at UT Austin. The syllabus covers Kirchhoff’s laws, node analysis, superposition and Thevenin equivalents, op-amps, capacitors, MOSFETs, frequency-domain analysis, complex impedance and Fourier series.

title: ECE 302: Introduction to Electrical Engineering
text: An ECE 302 MOSFET lab compared drain current across a range of gate voltages. The post-lab calculations estimated a 1.42 V threshold voltage and 9.38 mS transconductance; these are reported estimates.

title: ECE 302: Introduction to Electrical Engineering
text: An ECE 302 lab board design associated with Chris includes a KiCad schematic, PCB layout, and exported Gerber and drill files. The available evidence does not establish who performed each design step or whether the board was fabricated.

title: ECE 306: Introduction to Computing
text: In Fall 2024 ECE 306 work, Chris wrote LC-3 assembly programs using registers, masking, branching and memory access. One program adds two packed two’s-complement values and checks overflow; another sorts values in ascending order and invokes a comparison subroutine.

title: ECE 306: Introduction to Computing
text: Chris’s ECE 306 Lab 5 assembly implementation sets up a keyboard interrupt vector and interrupt enable, a system stack, and a return to user mode. A final demonstration result has not been established.

title: ECE 312H: Software Design and Implementation I
text: In Spring 2025 ECE 312H, Chris wrote C-style code for multiplying matrices both as row-major arrays and as dynamically allocated pointer arrays. The same assignment file creates a submatrix by excluding a selected row and column. The code documents pointer indexing and dynamic allocation.

title: ECE 312H: Software Design and Implementation I
text: Chris’s ECE 312H queue implementation uses dynamic memory for an integer queue and includes operations to duplicate, enqueue, dequeue, reverse, combine and free queues.

title: ECE 312H: Software Design and Implementation I
text: For an ECE 312H programming assignment, Chris wrote a C++ interpreter for a small language with text, output, variable and assignment commands. His implementation parses commands, stores variables in a map and evaluates prefix expressions.

title: ECE 319H: Introduction to Embedded Systems
text: In Spring 2025 ECE 319H, Chris and a lab partner wrote C code for an MSPM0 traffic-light controller. Their design defines a 13-state, pointer-based finite state machine with westbound, southbound and pedestrian signals and configures GPIO for LED outputs and switch inputs. Their individual contributions are not specified.

title: ECE 319H: Introduction to Embedded Systems
text: Chris and a lab partner’s ECE 319H lab code uses an MSPM0G3507, a slide potentiometer read through a 12-bit ADC, and an ST7735 display. A later joint lab design includes infrared transmission and UART reception using a FIFO queue. Individual contributions and hardware validation results have not been established.

title: ECE 316: Digital Logic Design
text: In ECE 316, Chris and a lab partner documented a BCD-to-seven-segment decoder for the Basys 3 FPGA. Their report includes a truth table, minimized equations, structural Verilog, a testbench stepping through all 16 input combinations, simulation waveforms and pin constraints.

title: ECE 316: Digital Logic Design
text: In a joint ECE 316 lab report, Chris and a partner designed clocked Verilog finite state machines, including a flight-attendant call system, a rising-edge detector and a four-digit multiplexed display controller. The report includes Verilog, testbenches and Basys 3 pin constraints.

title: ECE 316: Digital Logic Design
text: For an ECE 316 lab, Chris and a partner designed 4-bit ripple-carry and carry-lookahead adders with an enabled result register. Their report calculates critical-path delays of 28 ns and 17 ns respectively, with relative gate areas of 128 and 168. These are hand calculations under the lab’s assumed gate model, not measured hardware timings.

title: ECE 333T: Engineering Communication
text: In an ECE 333T classroom task-force simulation on AI-enabled campus surveillance, Chris represented a faculty perspective. His reflection says he proposed privacy safeguards against routine tracking, use in hiring, surveillance inside individual faculty offices and collection of intellectual property; he also helped the group discuss evidence review and oversight of a limited pilot.

title: UGS 104: FIG/TrIG Peer Mentor Preparation Course
text: In Spring 2026, Chris developed a proposed 50-minute peer-mentor seminar on internships and career fairs. The plan covered recruiting timelines, Engineering Expo preparation and job boards, with a paired activity for students to practice and give feedback on elevator pitches.

title: MATH 2318: Linear Algebra
text: In a MATH 2318 assessment, Chris analyzed the transformation T(A) = BA − AB on 2-by-2 matrices. His work checks linearity, derives a basis for the kernel, constructs a preimage to demonstrate range membership and gives a counterexample to show the transformation is not one-to-one.

title: ECE 125S: Internship in Electrical and Computer Engineering
text: Chris’s summer 2026 Celanese internship was associated with ECE 125S, which required a technical report connecting internship work to electrical and computer engineering coursework. Report submission and course credit have not been confirmed.

title: ECE 411: Circuit Theory
text: In a Fall 2025 ECE 411 lab, recorded RLC transient observations compared a 2-kilohm case described as overdamped with 510-ohm and 100-ohm cases described as underdamped. The lower resistance showed more oscillation. Individual contributions to the lab record are not specified.

title: ECE 411: Circuit Theory
text: An ECE 411 filter lab record tabulates output voltages and gain across frequencies from 10 Hz to 10 kHz. For the low-pass configuration, it reports 75 mV output at the calculated 79.58 Hz cutoff with a 100 mV reference input, versus an expected 70.7 mV; a second set of readings shows the contrasting high-pass response.

title: ECE 351K: Probability and Random Processes
text: Chris studied probability in ECE 351K in Fall 2026. Course topics included probability axioms, conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, independence, counting, discrete random variables, expectation, variance and joint distributions.

title: M 427L: Multivariable and Vector Calculus
text: Chris took M 427L at UT Austin in Spring 2026. Course material covered vectors in three dimensions, dot products, angles and vector projections.

title: CMS 344K: Lying and Deception
text: In Fall 2025, Chris’s CMS 344K course materials describe an examination of lying, deception, secrecy, privacy, disclosure and confidentiality in different contexts. The course also included an interview-based course project.

title: UGS 303: Drugs, Commerce, and Immigration in U.S.-Mexico Relations
text: In a UGS 303 essay, Chris analyzed a proposed partial opening of the U.S.–Mexico border and argued for reduced barrier investment and inspections. The essay uses cited sources to discuss trade, consumer costs, immigration and drug trafficking, illustrating evidence-based written argument rather than claiming the policy was enacted or its predicted effects measured.

title: STEAM Day Escape Room (Celanese)
text: During his 2026 Celanese internship, Chris built an Arduino Uno escape room for STEAM Day. Puzzles included a Morse-code LED, a Simon Says game using illuminated buttons, and a DHT22 temperature sensor. His résumé reports about 60 participants in rotating 15-minute sessions.

title: STEAM Day Escape Room (Celanese)
text: For the Celanese STEAM Day escape room, Chris combined Arduino C++ and Python. His résumé describes streaming sensor readings to a live Python display using pySerial and a fourth puzzle using MediaPipe Face Mesh to recognize a player’s facial expression.

title: Accuracy Prime and Motivated Reasoning Survey Experiment (CMS 345P)
text: For his Fall 2025 CMS 345P class project, Chris investigated whether an accuracy prime—asking people to reason as accurately and neutrally as possible—reduces motivated reasoning. He compared a treatment group with a control group on bias and changes in opinion about gun control.

title: Accuracy Prime and Motivated Reasoning Survey Experiment (CMS 345P)
text: In his CMS 345P survey experiment, Chris calculated each participant’s bias score, opinion change, and movement toward or away from the scale midpoint. He used two-tailed Welch’s t-tests to compare independent treatment and control groups.

title: Accuracy Prime and Motivated Reasoning Survey Experiment (CMS 345P)
text: Chris’s CMS 345P experiment had 37 respondents: 17 treatment and 20 control. Mean bias scores were 2.73 and 2.50; mean opinion changes were 0.59 and 0.40. The Welch tests found no statistically significant differences in bias, opinion change, or moderation (p = 0.86, 0.84, and 0.83 respectively). The predominantly young sample limits generalization.

title: Interview-Based Research Project (CMS 344K)
text: For a Fall 2025 CMS 344K project, Chris and a partner interviewed a law-enforcement professional about deception. Chris prepared questions about recognizing deception, the ethics of deception in interviews, and assisted lie detection. A final analysis was not available for review.

title: Evidence-Backed Portfolio Assistant (COE 379L Final Project)
text: For their Fall 2026 COE 379L final project, Chris and a partner proposed an evidence-backed portfolio assistant to answer questions about a person’s education, skills and experience using an owner-approved corpus. The team planned retrieval, citation checking and abstention when evidence is insufficient. As of late November 2026, the project was at the proposal and scaffold stage.

title: Evidence-Backed Portfolio Assistant (COE 379L Final Project)
text: The planned COE 379L portfolio assistant combines a Python backend, retrieval tools, a language model and a Lean validator. The design has the server track retrieved passage IDs and check the model’s proposed citations against them. The integration specification uses those IDs for internal checking and defines a plain-text browser reply; it does not specify displaying citations to visitors.

title: Evidence-Backed Portfolio Assistant (COE 379L Final Project)
text: For the proposed COE 379L portfolio assistant, Chris was assigned a Lean validator designed to reject malformed responses and answers whose paragraphs lack citations to passages retrieved for that request. The team also planned checks for abstentions and scripted validation cases. As of late November 2026, the checker was specified but not yet implemented.

title: Evidence-Backed Portfolio Assistant (COE 379L Final Project)
text: The proposed COE 379L portfolio assistant would be evaluated on factual accuracy, support from retrieved passages, coverage and appropriate abstention, including cases involving prompt injection. The team also planned scripted cases for valid and invalid validator inputs. Evaluation results were not yet available in late November 2026.

title: Evidence-Backed Portfolio Assistant (COE 379L Final Project)
text: The Fall 2026 COE 379L portfolio-assistant proposal assigns Chris the chat interface, owner-approved corpus, Lean validator, and validator test cases. His partner is assigned retrieval and model integration; both share integration, documentation and presentation. These are planned responsibilities in a two-person project.

title: Atlas Laboratory Agent (COE 379L Midterm Project)

His résumé lists Pydantic and pytest and describes retrieval-augmented generation, tool calling, structured outputs, and authorization and response-grounding checks within a bounded agent loop. The repository includes policy retrieval, validation, a simulated environment and automated tests.

title: Atlas Laboratory Agent (COE 379L Midterm Project)
text: The saved public benchmark for Chris’s Atlas laboratory agent contains six scenarios and reports a 1.0 success rate, zero invalid structured responses, zero unsafe action attempts, and an average of 2.67 tool calls. These figures describe the saved public scenarios, not performance in a real laboratory.

text: In Chris’s ECE 316 Lab 6 stopwatch/timer design, button inputs pass through synchronization and debounce logic. The Verilog generates separate 10 ms counting and 1 ms display-scanning enables and converts the counter value to display digits.
